Games Theory:
Strategy, Conflict & Decision-Making

Example: A Dice 
Game
• Two players A and B each roll a die.
• The sum of the two rolls determines the
payoff:
• If Sum is Odd → A Wins : Player B
pays Player A the value of the sum.
• If Sum is Even → B Wins: Player A
pays Player B the value of the sum
(recorded as negative for A).
Dr. Soniya Dhama, RGIPT

3 −4 5 −6 7 −8 9

5 −6 7 −8 9 −10 11
6 7 −8 9 −10 11 −12
The Payoff Matrix:
• This 6×6 matrix is a rectangular game.
• Each row is a strategy for A (values 1–6)
• Each column is a strategy for B.
• The entry aᵢⱼ is the amount B pays to A.
• A negative entry means A pays B.
Example:
• A throws 1, B throws 6 → sum = 7 (odd) →
A receives Rs 7.
• A throws 2, B throws 4 → sum = 6 (even) →
A pays Rs 6, recorded as −6.

Key Definitions
Game: 
A set of rules followed by players with 
conflicting objectives.
Game theory (introduced by von 
Neumann): Studies rational decision￾making under conflict.
Rectangular Game: 
A two-player game where A has m
strategies and B has n strategies, 
represented by an m × n payoff 
matrix [aᵢⱼ].
2-Person Zero-Sum Game: 
A game where one player's gain 
exactly equals the other's loss.
Total received by both players at each 
play = aᵢⱼ + (−aᵢⱼ) = 0.
Strategy: 
A predetermined rule dictating which 
course of action a player takes at each 
turn, potentially based on prior moves 
and the opponent's behavior.
Dr. Soniya Dhama, RGIPT

Pure Strategy vs. 
Mixed Strategy
Pure Strategy: 
• Each player plays exactly 
one strategy per game.
• Deterministic. 
• Works when a saddle point 
exists.
Dr. Soniya Dhama, RGIPT
Mixed Strategy: 
• Each player assigns probabilities
to their strategies.
• A player A with m strategies, is 
associated with probabilities 
(𝑥₁, 𝑥₂, … , 𝑥ₘ) where each 𝑥ᵢ
≥ 0 and Σ𝑥ᵢ = 1.
• Used when no saddle point 
exists.

Principle of Dominance (6 Rules)
In a 2-person zero-sum game,
Player A maximizes while Player
B minimizes the payoff. The
payoff matrix can often be
simplified before solving.
Dominance rules let us eliminate
rows and columns that a rational
player would never choose —
shrinking the problem without
losing the optimal solution.
• Dominated strategies are assigned zero probability in the optimal mixed strategy.

Rule I:
Row Dominance — Direct
The Condition
Row p dominates row q if:
𝒂𝒑𝒋 ≥ 𝒂𝒒𝒋, for all 𝒋 = 𝟏, … , 𝒏
Player A, as the maximizer, will never play a
dominated row. The optimal strategy sets 𝑥𝑞 = 0 and
row q is deleted.
IDENTIFY
Find a row where every entry is ≥ every 
corresponding entry of another row.
ELIMINATE
Set the dominated row's probability to zero 
and remove it from the matrix.
SIMPLIFY
Continue solving the reduced matrix.

Column Dominance — Direct
The Condition

𝒂𝒊𝒓 ≥ 𝒂𝒊𝒔, for all 𝒊 = 𝟏, … , 𝒎
Player B is the minimizer (a higher-valued column is
worse), so they avoid the dominating column. The optimal
strategy sets 𝑦𝑟 = 0 and column r is deleted.

Rule I vs. Rule II: 
A deletes dominated rows (lower values). B deletes dominating columns (higher values).

RULE V — ROWS
A convex combination of rows dominates 
another row. 
Delete each row of the combination one at
a time, solve the resulting game, and select
whichever deletion yields the maximum value
of 𝑣 (saddle value).
RULE VI — COLUMNS
A convex combination of columns is 
dominated by another column. 
Delete each column of the combination
one at a time, solve the resulting game, and
select whichever deletion yields the
minimum value of 𝑣 (saddle value).
When it's unclear which member of the combination to remove, these rules provide a decision procedure:
Rules V and VI are trial-based: solve multiple sub-problems and pick the optimal result — max for A, min for B.
